items_missed: Opened with the wrong name — 'Hi Sara, this is Teresa from Einstein Moving Company com. Am I speaking with Christian?' She recovered inside the same breath, but the customer's first impression was a rep reading off the wrong record.

Never asked 'how are you today?' — and worse, the customer asked her. 'Yes, you are. How's it going?' got no answer at all; she went straight into 'Hi, there so yes, we noticed that you booked your move online.' That is a social opening handed to her and stepped over, and it set the procedural tone for the whole call.

No agenda statement. 'I was just reaching out to conduct your kickoff call. So is this a good time?' names the call type but gives no roadmap and no timeframe — the customer never learned what would be covered or that a price conversation was coming.
Additional stops never asked.

What's-included list never given. Not gas, not the truck, not taxes, not insurance, not blankets, not pads, not bands, not tools. She went from '$104 per hour per mover... so we're looking at $208 an hour' directly to the 2.5-hour minimum. The customer has a rate and a floor and no idea what arrives for it.
Disassembly and reassembly never mentioned as included — on a call where she had just spent two minutes on a king bed and a wall-mounted 65-inch OLED.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. This is the highest-value miss across all eight calls this week, because the customer volunteered his single biggest anxiety unprompted: 'The TV is, is relatively fragile. It's a rather large TV about 65 inches and it's pretty thin as well,' and confirmed it is an OLED. She responded with logistics — take it off the wall, we can box it — and never once said that every move carries up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage. The customer named the fear and the answer was in her script and never came out.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, and she handed him a two-hour arrival window in the same breath: 'that can be in the start window. As I can see here is a 12:30 AM to 2:30 PM start window.' A window with no guarantee attached is an obligation on the customer, not a promise from us.
Clock start never explained — nothing about the clock starting on-site when the contract opens.

No estimate was given at all. No dollar figure, no hour range, no typical benchmark for a one-bedroom, nothing. On a move that is two days away and already booked, the customer's entire understanding of what this will cost is '$208 an hour' and 'a two and a half hour minimum.' Every scoring bullet in Section 5 that depends on a quote existing is a miss by default.
Truck never mentioned anywhere on the call — not in inclusions, not in the crew description.

The fourth floor, the elevator, the twenty-foot ground walk and the forty-yard fourth-floor hallway walk were all captured in detail and none of them were ever converted into time. She ran the best access interview in the batch and told the customer nothing about what any of it meant.
Drive time never mentioned. 1515 South Lamar to 201 East Fourth Street is a downtown Austin run and the customer was never told whether it is billable.
Traffic never mentioned — a mid-day move into 201 East Fourth Street, downtown, and no mention of it.
Assembly and disassembly time never discussed, on an identified king bed.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used anywhere.
Save Your Ass entirely absent — 0/10. See the coaching note; a booked move two days out with a forty-yard fourth-floor carry is the highest-ROI setting for this speech in the batch.

No email handoff. She never said she would send anything. She collected two unit numbers, an inventory list, box counts and two walk distances on this call and none of it was committed to writing or confirmed back to the customer.
BOLDED-details framing absent, and the 'reply with any corrections' verification ask absent.
Hours and how to reach us never given — 'please feel free to reach back out to us' with no number, no channel and no hours, two days before a move.
Customer's name never used cleanly. She opened with the wrong one, asked 'Am I speaking with Christian?' once, and used 'sir' at the close. Zero of the 3+ standard.
top_strength: Therese runs the best access and specialty-item interview in this entire batch, and several of her questions are ones no other rep this week thought to ask. She is the only person of the eight to ask whether the building's elevator can be held: 'will the elevator be reserved for the move by the way.' That question prevents one of the most common real-world overruns on a high-rise move and it is not even on the rubric. She is also the only rep to ask the additional-spaces question in its full form: 'Do you have additional spaces that we need to move, move like any items from a balcony storage closet or a study?' And she mapped the walk in two segments rather than one, which is how you actually estimate a fourth-floor carry — first 'what is the block distance from where we can park the truck to the elevator of the first floor' (twenty feet), then 'once we get to the fourth floor is the apartment right there, or is there a walk involved there as well?' which produced 'probably about forty yards.' She gave the customer room to think for that answer rather than filling the silence, which is why she got a real number instead of 'not far.' Her specialty-item probing is the best moment on any call this week. She opened it properly — 'any special considerations in terms of the furniture items that will be moving for you? Anything that's particularly heavy or large or fragile' — surfaced the 65-inch OLED, and then did not stop: she asked whether it was an OLED specifically, whether it was wall-mounted, and whether he still had the original box, then offered real help: 'you can definitely take it off the wall before the movers get there or we can take it off the wall for you if you'd like and we can also help you box it up since it is a larger TV.' And then she asked the follow-up almost every rep skips: 'Is there anything else that might be a little cumbersome or awkward even?' That second ask is what surfaced the king bed and the large TV console — three quarters of the difficult inventory on this job came out of a question she did not have to ask. She also used the benchmark framing correctly on boxes ('typically for a one bedroom apartment we would usually see about fifteen to 25 boxes. Do you feel like you'd fall within that standard range?'), which anchors the customer instead of making them guess cold.
coaching_note: Interviewing note on how this was graded: this is a post-booking kickoff call, not a prospecting call, so the Section 7 booking-attempt and no-deposit bullets were granted as N/A — the sale is already closed. Everything else on the 85-point rubric applies and was graded normally, because this is the call where the estimate actually gets built and the expectations get set. Highest-leverage fix, and it is a strange one to write: Therese ran the best intake in the batch and then produced nothing from it. She collected the floor, the elevator, whether the elevator could be reserved, a twenty-foot ground carry, a forty-yard hallway carry, a king bed, a TV console, a 65-inch OLED and a twenty-box estimate — and then gave the customer no estimate at all. No hours, no dollar figure, no typical range, not even 'most one-bedrooms like yours run three to four hours.' This move is two days away and the customer's entire financial picture is '$208 an hour' and 'a two and a half hour minimum.' That is how a booked move becomes a billing dispute: he will do the same arithmetic every customer does, land on $520, and then be billed for four and a half hours because of a carry she measured and never mentioned. Note that this is the same branch and the same failure mode as the Daniel Behseresht service-recovery call in this week's sample — a North Austin job quoted at five and a half hours that ran ten and cost $777 in refund. The discovery work is genuinely excellent; the gap is that none of it reaches the customer. Every access fact she collects should end in a sentence the customer hears: 'so with the fourth floor, the elevator, and that forty-yard walk on your floor, I'd budget four to five hours, roughly $830 to $1,040 — and we only bill for the time we actually use.' Second priority: No Worries Damage Coverage. The customer told her, unprompted, that his biggest concern was a thin 65-inch OLED. That is the most direct invitation to deliver the $2,000 coverage on any call this week and she gave him logistics instead. The line: 'And for what it's worth on the TV — every move comes with No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse anything we damage, which is well past the 60 cents a pound the state requires. So if anything happens to it, you're covered.' That is the sentence that turns an anxious booked customer into a referral. The what's-included list is missing entirely too, which is a five-second fix and worth two rubric points: gas, truck, taxes, insurance, blankets, wrap, bands and tools. Third: Save Your Ass is a zero, and a booked move two days out is the single best moment for it in the whole sample — the customer still has 48 hours to act, and every minute saved on a forty-yard fourth-floor carry is real money. He even opened the door by offering to take the TV off the wall himself. 'That's perfect, and here's the rest of it — anything small you can carry down yourself before Thursday comes straight off the clock. The loose stuff in drawers, the closet odds and ends, pictures off the walls. On a fourth-floor carry like yours that's where the hours actually go. Does that make sense?' Fourth, a smaller thing that matters: he asked 'How's it going?' and she did not answer. Two days from a move, that is the customer offering warmth and getting a checklist back. Answer it, and use his name — she never said it once.
phone_presence_notes: A genuinely good listener — she let the customer think through the forty-yard walk without filling the silence, chased the OLED thread properly, and offered real help boxing it — but the register is procedural throughout: she opened with the wrong name, did not answer his 'How's it going?', never used his name once across 7.2 minutes, leaned on 'Okay, perfect' roughly ten times as her only acknowledgment, and never converted his stated worry about the TV into any reassurance.
audio_review_reason: A 3 driven largely by register rather than content, which is the hardest thing to judge from text. The 'Okay, perfect' loop and the unreturned 'How's it going?' read as checklist-working on paper, but Therese may well sound warm and attentive in delivery — and her listening behavior in the transcript (waiting through his pauses, following the TV thread) suggests she might. Getting that right matters because the coaching is different: if she sounds warm, the fix is purely structural (give an estimate, deliver No Worries); if she sounds flat, it is both. Also worth confirming whether she actually addressed the customer as 'Sara' at the open or whether that is a transcription artifact, and whether the arrival window given as '12:30 AM to 2:30 PM' was stated coherently to a customer whose move is in two days.
